findings.name: process-global-mutation
findings.message: warnings.catch_warnings() swaps the global warnings filter and is documented as not thread-safe
findings.why: os.environ, locale, warnings filters, signal handlers, sys.path, the recursion limit and numpy's error state are shared by every thread in the process. A library that flips them affects unrelated threads. No amount of locking inside the library can fix this, because the observers are outside it.
findings.fix: Prefer an explicit parameter or a context object. If the global really must change, do it once at import/configure time, or document the call as not-thread-safe and expose a non-global alternative.

findings.name: lazy-init-race
findings.message: `_initial_defencoding` is lazily initialised with an unsynchronised check-then-act
findings.why: `if X is None: X = expensive()` is two bytecode-separated operations. Under free-threading N threads can all observe None and all run the initialiser. That duplicates side effects (open files, spawned threads, registered handles) and, worse, lets one thread publish an object that another thread is still mutating.
findings.fix: Guard with a module-level lock and re-check inside it, or precompute the value at import time, or use functools.cache (whose C implementation is atomic) when the initialiser is genuinely pure.

findings.name: check-then-act-container
findings.message: `not in HANDLERS` test followed by a mutation of `HANDLERS`
findings.snippet:
if vcs not in HANDLERS:
    HANDLERS[vcs] = {}
findings.why: `if k not in cache: cache[k] = compute(k)` is not atomic. Two threads can both miss, both compute, and both store. If the stored object carries identity (a connection, a lock, a registry entry) callers end up holding different objects that were supposed to be the same one.
findings.fix: Use dict.setdefault() / collections.defaultdict, which are atomic at the C level, or hold a lock across the test and the mutation.

if _table_mod is None:

findings.name: process-global-mutation
findings.message: `os.chdir()` mutates the process working directory
findings.why: os.environ, locale, warnings filters, signal handlers, sys.path, the recursion limit and numpy's error state are shared by every thread in the process. A library that flips them affects unrelated threads. No amount of locking inside the library can fix this, because the observers are outside it.
findings.fix: Prefer an explicit parameter or a context object. If the global really must change, do it once at import/configure time, or document the call as not-thread-safe and expose a non-global alternative.

findings.name: read-modify-write
findings.message: `FigureCanvasBase._last_blit_background_id +=` is a non-atomic read-modify-write on shared state
findings.why: `counter += 1` compiles to LOAD / BINARY_OP / STORE. With the GIL these rarely interleaved; without it they interleave constantly and increments are silently lost. This is the single most reproducible free-threading bug.
findings.fix: Use itertools.count().__next__, a lock, or move the counter into per-thread state and aggregate at the end.

findings.name: lazy-init-race
findings.message: `_application` is lazily initialised with an unsynchronised check-then-act
findings.why: `if X is None: X = expensive()` is two bytecode-separated operations. Under free-threading N threads can all observe None and all run the initialiser. That duplicates side effects (open files, spawned threads, registered handles) and, worse, lets one thread publish an object that another thread is still mutating.
findings.fix: Guard with a module-level lock and re-check inside it, or precompute the value at import time, or use functools.cache (whose C implementation is atomic) when the initialiser is genuinely pure.

That duplicates side effects (open files, spawned threads, registered handles) and, worse, lets one thread publish an object that another thread is still mutating.
findings.fix: Guard with a module-level lock and re-check inside it, or precompute the value at import time, or use functools.cache (whose C implementation is atomic) when the initialiser is genuinely pure.

findings.why: `if k not in cache: cache[k] = compute(k)` is not atomic. Two threads can both miss, both compute, and both store. If the stored object carries identity (a connection, a lock, a registry entry) callers end up holding different objects that were supposed to be the same one.

findings.name: process-global-mutation
findings.message: `warnings.simplefilter()` mutates the global warnings filter
findings.why: os.environ, locale, warnings filters, signal handlers, sys.path, the recursion limit and numpy's error state are shared by every thread in the process. A library that flips them affects unrelated threads. No amount of locking inside the library can fix this, because the observers are outside it.
findings.fix: Prefer an explicit parameter or a context object. If the global really must change, do it once at import/configure time, or document the call as not-thread-safe and expose a non-global alternative.

findings.name: save-mutate-restore
findings.message: `os.environ` is changed and then restored in a finally block
findings.why: The save/mutate/restore idiom is only correct if nothing else runs meanwhile. Under free-threading another thread executes inside the window and sees the temporary value; two threads doing it concurrently restore each other's saved value and leave the global permanently wrong.
findings.fix: Thread the value through as a parameter, or move it to a threading.local / contextvars.ContextVar so each thread has its own copy.

findings.name: read-modify-write
findings.message: `_trim_arity_call_line` is read and written back without synchronisation
findings.why: `counter += 1` compiles to LOAD / BINARY_OP / STORE. With the GIL these rarely interleaved; without it they interleave constantly and increments are silently lost. This is the single most reproducible free-threading bug.
findings.fix: Use itertools.count().__next__, a lock, or move the counter into per-thread state and aggregate at the end.
